The latter are also an alternative where fluoro- quinolone resistance exists;3,4 this is an increasing prob- lem, particularly in Asia, but most fluoroquinolone-resist- ant strains seen in the UK retain their sensitivity to cephalosporins, and to azithromycin, which is another al- ternative.5 Combination regimens have been investigat- ed,4 but a study in patients infected with strains showing both multidrug resistance and reduced susceptibility to fluoroquinolones found that azithromycin alone was pref- erable to azithromycin plus ofloxacin.6 Interestingly, there is some evidence that as fluoroquinolone resistance spreads, sensitivity to some of the older drugs used to treat the disease, such as chloramphenicol, may be returning.7,8 Although fluoroquinolones are not generally indicated in children because of potential toxicity, WHO considers that their benefits in typhoid fever outweigh any putative risk.3 Azithromycin may also be given.3 In pregnancy a beta- lactam such as ampicillin or one of the cephalosporins may be preferable,3 although there are reports of the successful use of fluoroquinolones. WHO also suggests that although there is no evidence to suggest harm, azithromycin should not be used in pregnant or nursing women if alternatives are available.3 Patients who develop mental changes should be evaluated for meningitis; if typhoid meningitis is suspected, high- dose intravenous dexamethasone should be given in addi- tion to antibacterial treatment.3 On recovery, typhoid patients may continue to excrete S. typhi in the faeces or urine for several weeks. Unlike these convalescent carriers, some 1 to 5% of patients become chronic carriers3 who may excrete S. typhi for years with- out any symptoms; eradication is difficult and prolonged treatment is necessary. An increased risk of biliary-tract and bile-related cancers has been associated with chronic carriage of S. typhi, and the importance of eradication has been emphasised.9 Typhoid vaccines are used for the prevention of typhoid fever. Paratyphoid fever is less common and generally milder than typhoid fever. Treatment is similar. 1. Parry CM, et al. Typhoid fever. N Engl J Med 2002; 347: 1770–82. 2. Rowe B, et al. Multidrug-resistant Salmonella typhi: a world- wide epidemic. Clin Infect Dis 1997; 24 (suppl 1): S106–S109. 3. WHO.
